projects.title: Agentic AI Platform
projects.description: An internal platform for building multi-agent workflows on top of local and hosted LLMs — tool use, memory, guardrails, and human-in-the-loop review for mobility and operations teams.
projects.oneLiner: Enterprise AI that reaches past chat — agents that use tools, keep context, and hand risky work back to a human.
projects.problem: Most enterprise AI stops at a chat window: it can answer, but it can't act, it forgets everything between sessions, and there is no safe way to let it touch a real system. The teams who would benefit most — mobility operations — need AI that reaches into tools and data, while staying inside limits a business can defend.
approach: Built an internal platform for composing multi-agent workflows rather than one-off bots, so teams assemble what they need instead of commissioning a new integration each time.
Gave agents real capability — tool use and memory — so they can carry out a task end to end instead of returning text for a human to re-key.
Wrapped every workflow in guardrails, with human-in-the-loop review that triggers when the risk of an action is too high.
Ran it on both local and hosted models, so sensitive workloads can stay private without giving up frontier capability elsewhere.
projects.outcome: A platform mobility and operations teams build on, where agents do real work under explicit limits — and the first step toward the accountability layer autonomous agents will need.
story: Agents are the next interface — and the next attack surface. Most enterprise AI still stops at chat. We're building past that: multi-agent workflows that can actually reach into tools, remember context, and hand work back to a human when the risk is too high.

The bigger bet: as agents get more autonomy, someone has to build the accountability layer around them — systems that catch bad behaviour, correct it, and only then hand autonomy back. This platform is the first honest step toward that.

projects.title: CUBONIC — Digital Infrastructure for Last-Mile Mobility
projects.description: Building CUBONIC's digital infrastructure from the ground up — connecting the vehicle and its autonomous driving stack to the wider ecosystem behind sustainable last-mile mobility: autonomous, connected electric light commercial vehicles.
projects.oneLiner: The digital backbone for autonomous, connected electric vans — built from the ground up.
projects.problem: A new vehicle programme is not just a vehicle. An autonomous, connected eLCV only delivers last-mile mobility if there is a digital layer underneath it — connecting what the vehicle knows to the operators, customers and systems around it. At CUBONIC that layer did not exist yet; it had to be built from the ground up, in parallel with the vehicle itself.
approach: Built the digital infrastructure from zero rather than assembling it from off-the-shelf fleet tooling, so it fits an autonomous vehicle rather than a conventional one.
Connected the vehicle and its autonomous driving stack into the wider CUBONIC ecosystem, so vehicle data becomes operational capability.
Led AI strategy, private LLM deployment and agentic systems as part of the same backbone — the platform, the local model stack and the governance model are one programme, not three.
Kept it aimed at the actual business outcome: sustainable last-mile delivery that works commercially, not a technology demonstration.
projects.outcome: The digital foundation the CUBONIC vehicle and ecosystem run on — and the platform the agentic and private-LLM work is built into.

projects.title: AutoScout24 Mobile Apps
projects.description: Head of Product for the native apps of Europe's largest car marketplace — search, favorites, price-drop alerts, dealer contact and selling flows across 2M+ listings, plus the AutoTrader and Gebrauchtwagen.de white-label apps. Led 4 senior PMs and 24 engineers; grew organic user acquisition 30% across European markets, doubled engagement, improved conversion 23% and lifted app advertising revenue 10%.
projects.oneLiner: Europe's largest car marketplace, in your pocket — four apps, one team, four numbers moved at once.
projects.role: Head of Product / Head of Apps
projects.problem: Own the vision, strategy and roadmap for the native apps of Europe's largest car marketplace — iOS, Android and the white-label apps (AutoTrader, Gebrauchtwagen.de) — and move four numbers at once: organic acquisition, engagement, conversion and app advertising revenue. All of it across multiple European markets, on a marketplace where private buyers and professional dealers want very different things from the same product.
approach: Made search and discovery the core loop — filters, saved searches and a notepad for favourites, so returning to a shortlist is one tap rather than a new search.
Turned price-drop alerts into the retention engine: push notifications on saved cars bring users back at exactly the moment their decision changes.
Closed the buyer–dealer gap with direct dealer contact and verified, authentic dealer reviews on every listing.
Opened the sell side in-app — photo upload and a free value check, so listing a car takes minutes on a phone.
Ran AutoScout24, AutoTrader and Gebrauchtwagen.de from one white-label platform, so a single team's work shipped to every market.
Kept decisions data-informed, pairing product analytics with insight from the international offices and business stakeholders.
projects.outcome: Organic user acquisition up 30% across European markets, app engagement doubled, conversion up 23% and app advertising revenue up 10% — delivered by a lean app team of 4 senior PMs and 24 engineers owning a business result at marketplace scale.
story: Two million listings. Millions of users. One iOS and one Android app carrying the whole marketplace in your pocket — plus the white-label AutoTrader and Gebrauchtwagen.de apps on the same codebase.

Coming from Cluno, I brought the same instinct: connect the two journeys — the buyer's journey and the vehicle's journey — inside one engine. Every price-drop notification, every dealer contact, every save is a touch point in a much larger system.

Numbers moved: +30% organic acquisition across markets, 2× engagement, +23% conversion, +10% in-app ad revenue. Senior PMs, app marketing and engineers. The proudest part isn't the metrics — it's that a lean app team owned a business result at that scale.

projects.title: Local LLM Stack
projects.description: Private, on-prem LLM deployment stack for regulated data — model routing, quantization, evaluation harness, and observability, so sensitive workloads never leave the perimeter.
projects.oneLiner: Frontier AI on regulated data — private by architecture, not by policy.
projects.problem: Regulated data cannot leave the perimeter, but the useful models mostly live outside it. The usual answer is a policy promising nobody will paste anything sensitive into a chatbot — which is not an architecture, and does not survive contact with a deadline.
approach: Routed requests across model sizes, so each workload runs on the smallest model that actually does the job.
Tuned quantization per workload to make on-prem deployment economic instead of theoretical.
Built an evaluation harness that tells you when a model regresses — the difference between shipping AI and hoping.
Added observability so nothing runs blind, and every answer can be traced.
projects.outcome: Sensitive workloads stay inside the perimeter by architecture. Private deployment became a default option for the business rather than a special case.
story: In 2008, I dreamt of a world where I could type in plain English and get machine code back. In 2017, I trained my first neural net on industrial CT scans. In 2025, that dream is a product problem: how do you deploy it without leaking a single row of regulated data?

This stack answers that. Model routing across sizes, quantization tuned per workload, an evaluation harness that actually tells you when a model regresses, and observability so nothing runs blind. Sensitive workloads stay inside the perimeter — by architecture, not by policy.
projects.coverCaption: private by design, zero perimeter exit

projects.title: Cluno — Partner Platform & Business Engine
projects.description: One platform connecting Cluno with its whole partner ecosystem — 131 dealerships, logistics carriers, refurbishers and vehicle assessors across Germany, with 100% dealership adoption and nearly 1,000 vehicles ordered through it. Order confirmation, scheduling, digital handover protocols, invoicing, one-click remarketing auctions via Auto1 and vehicle-health reporting replaced email-and-spreadsheet workflows, letting a lean operations team run a growing subscription fleet. Cluno was later acquired by Cazoo.
projects.oneLiner: The operating engine for a car-subscription business — one platform for every partner, from order to remarketing.
projects.problem: Cluno was a car-subscription startup with real ambition and no operating engine: dealerships, logistics carriers, refurbishers and assessors were all coordinated by email and spreadsheets. That works until volume arrives — then every new vehicle costs manual effort, and growth is capped by the operations team's inbox.
approach: Owned the whole journey from the moment a customer says 'I want this car' — Schufa credit checks, billing, insurance, refurbishment, remarketing, logistics and handover.
Built one partner portal for dealerships, carriers, refurbishers and assessors, replacing email-and-spreadsheet workflows with order confirmation, scheduling and invoicing.
Added one-click remarketing auctions via Auto1, so end-of-life vehicles left the fleet without a manual process.
Shipped digital handover protocols and vehicle-health reporting, plus the customer's iOS and Android apps.
Stitched the two parallel journeys — the customer's lifecycle and the vehicle's lifecycle — into a single system.
projects.outcome: A lean operations team could run a growing subscription fleet: 131 dealerships connected with 100% adoption and nearly 1,000 vehicles ordered through the platform. That engine is what Cazoo acquired.
story: After a decade in embedded systems and industrial software, I made a hard pivot into the cloud. Cluno was the landing site — a small car-subscription startup in Munich with big ambitions and no operating engine.

My job was to build that engine. Not rebuild — build. From the moment a customer said 'I want this car,' I owned the whole journey: Schufa credit checks, billing, insurance, refurb, remarketing via Auto1, logistics, and a fully digital handover with zero paper. On top of that, iOS and Android apps for the customer, and a partner portal for the dealers, carriers, and refurbishers.
This is where I stopped talking about MVPs and started talking about MLPs — Most Lovable Products. Ship small, but ship something people love. Love means trust. You keep building on trust.

The real insight of Cluno: two journeys running in parallel — the customer's lifecycle and the vehicle's lifecycle — meeting for a while, then parting. Stitch them into one system and you have a business engine. That engine is what Cazoo bought.

projects.title: Extend3D — Werklicht AR Projection
projects.description: Architect and scrum master for Extend3D's Werklicht laser/video projection system — augmented reality that projects CAD data directly onto physical parts on the automotive shop floor. Qt, C++ and the CGM modeler kernel, including a 3D data framework importing GOM, Polyworks and SpaceClaim formats.
projects.oneLiner: Augmented reality for the shop floor — CAD data projected straight onto the physical part.
projects.role: Architect & Scrum Master (effectively CTO/CPO for the client)
projects.problem: Extend3D had a beautiful piece of mathematics — an algorithm to transform 3D into 2D and project it back onto real objects at true scale — plus the hardware to do it. What they did not have was the software or the product thinking to turn it into something an automotive plant could use.
approach: Acted as architect and scrum master, effectively the CTO/CPO for someone else's company as a third party.
Built the Werklicht laser and video projection system on Qt, C++ and the CGM modeler kernel.
Wrote a 3D data framework importing the formats customers actually had — GOM, Polyworks and SpaceClaim.
Worked startup-style: nothing on the shelf, every test rig ordered and every invoice chased personally.
projects.outcome: An operator on the line sees the design overlaid on the part itself — CAD projected directly onto a car body or aircraft panel. Still the reference point for what 'AR on the shop floor' should mean.
story: Extend3D was three people with a beautiful piece of math — an algorithm to transform 3D into 2D and project it back onto real objects at real scale. They had the hardware and the mathematics. They needed the software and the product thinking.

This was my first taste of being effectively the CTO/CPO for someone else's company — as a third party, from Merz. Nothing was on the shelf: every test rig had to be ordered, every invoice chased. Big-company reflexes don't work in a startup.

What we built projects CAD data straight onto a car body or aircraft panel — the operator sees the design overlaid on the part itself. That collaboration is still what I think of when someone says 'AR on the shop floor.'

projects.title: Cazoo — Asset Financing & European Rollout
projects.description: After Cazoo's acquisition of Cluno, led product for asset financing, fleet management and car production — the systems that financed and tracked the subscription fleet. Contributed to a 30% rise in subscription revenue and a 50% improvement in vehicle contribution margin, and supported the Cazoo retail launch across 5 European markets.
projects.oneLiner: Financing and moving a subscription fleet across Europe — while the company was going public.
projects.role: Senior Product Manager — asset financing, fleet & production
projects.problem: Cluno was acquired by Cazoo mid-flight and Munich became the European HQ. The subscription fleet now had to be financed across multiple credit lines and moved across borders — while the company listed on the NYSE and every market applied its own regulation.
approach: Stood up asset financing across multiple credit lines, and the systems that tracked what each vehicle was worth.
Built first-mile, mid-mile and last-mile logistics for whole truckloads of cars across Germany, France and Spain — refurbishment centres, distribution hubs and home delivery.
Took regulation market by market rather than waiting for one perfect pan-European product.
Supported the Cazoo retail proposition launch across five European markets.
projects.outcome: Subscription revenue up 30% and vehicle contribution margin up 50%, with the retail proposition live in five markets — delivered while the business was being rebuilt around an IPO.
story: Cluno was acquired by Cazoo mid-flight. Munich became the European HQ. Overnight I was reporting into the Cazoo CPO, in the room for the IPO conversations, with equity that suddenly meant working for yourself as well as the company.

Flying a rocket ship while it's being built. That's the honest description. We stood up asset financing across multiple credit lines, and built the first-mile / mid-mile / last-mile logistics for whole truckloads of cars across Germany, France, and Spain — refurb centres, distribution hubs, home delivery.

The hardest part wasn't the tech; it was regulation, region by region. You couldn't wait for a perfect product. You shipped what worked, learned, iterated. +30% subscription revenue. +50% vehicle contribution margin. Retail launch in 5 markets.

projects.title: Avionics & Safety-Critical Systems
projects.description: Engine Indication and Crew Alert System for the pilot's primary display of NAL's SARAS aircraft — flight management, GPS position, fuel indication and ground-maintenance modules in C++ under DO-178B; assembly-level V&V of the TI DSP code in Meggitt's secondary flight display; and C firmware for Anderson-Negele food & pharma sensor systems.
projects.oneLiner: Software that had to fly — the pilot's primary display, under DO-178B.
projects.problem: Avionics software has no tolerance for cleverness. The Engine Indication and Crew Alert System drives the pilot's primary display on NAL's SARAS aircraft — flight management, GPS position, fuel indication, ground maintenance — in real time, under DO-178B, where every line has to be justified.
approach: Built the EICAS modules in C++ under DO-178B: flight management, GPS position, fuel indication and ground maintenance.
Performed assembly-level verification and validation of the TI DSP code in Meggitt's secondary flight display — six months of hunting McCabe complexity in code written by teams in the UK.
Owned an embedded project end to end for Anderson-Negele: a microcontroller inside a food-and-pharma sensor acting as a mini-router — turbidity and viscosity readings out over I²C, Wi-Fi and RS-232.
Became the technical anchor for a small team — leadership earned through the work rather than granted by title.
projects.outcome: Three safety-critical programmes delivered, and a permanent change in how I read a function. It also showed me the limit I wanted to escape: with real-time constraints, the memory budget is the point — I wanted problems where the product was.
story: My first job out of college. Software that had to fly. EICAS — the pilot's primary display for NAL's SARAS aircraft — under DO-178B, with all the discipline that implies. Flight management, GPS position, fuel indication, ground maintenance. C++, real-time, no room for cleverness.

This was also my first taste of leadership: not as a manager with disciplinary authority, but as the technical anchor for a small group of friends. Mentoring, guiding, showing them where to look. It stuck as my definition of leadership — earn it through the work.
Then came six months of code review — hunting McCabe complexity in code written by teams in the UK. Boring, but it permanently changed how I read a function.

In 2010, Anderson-Negele: a one-man-army embedded project. A microcontroller inside a food-and-pharma sensor, acting as a mini-router — turbidity and viscosity readings out to I²C for the display, over Wi-Fi for subscribers, over RS-232 for downstream systems. First time I owned something end to end.
By the end of this chapter I was frustrated. Real-time constraints meant I couldn't build big systems. So I started looking for problems where the memory budget wasn't the point — the product was.

projects.title: AI Strategy & Governance
projects.description: A pragmatic AI operating model: opportunity mapping, capability roadmap, risk & governance framework, and vendor vs. build decisions — turning executive intent into shipped systems.
projects.oneLiner: From 'we know we need AI' to shipped systems — an operating model a CFO can defend.
projects.problem: Every executive team lands on the same curve: they know they need AI, they don't know where to start, and they don't want to become someone else's training data. The gap is rarely technology — it's the absence of an operating model that connects intent to something shipped.
approach: Mapped opportunities against real business outcomes — save cost, save time — rather than against what demos well.
Built a capability roadmap that respects the systems and skills already in the building.
Wrote a governance and risk framework a CFO can defend, not just an engineering team.
Made honest build-vs-buy calls that don't optimise for looking impressive.
projects.outcome: A repeatable path from executive intent to systems in production — the framework behind the agentic platform and the private LLM stack.
story: Every executive team I meet is somewhere on the same curve: 'we know we need AI, we don't know where to start, and we don't want to become someone else's training data.'

This is the framework I use to move them from intent to shipped systems — opportunity mapping against real business outcomes (save cost, save time — that's what an engineer does), a capability roadmap that respects what already exists, a governance and risk model that a CFO can defend, and honest build-vs-buy calls that don't optimize for looking impressive.

projects.title: Digital Handover & Damage Reporting
projects.description: A three-step digital protocol replacing paper checklists for every vehicle transaction — 3,700+ digital handovers, 54% of them home deliveries, and a beta rollout with 100% successful handovers. Real-time handover status in Salesforce, plus in-app damage reporting with dynamic questionnaires, photos and location sharing that cut per-unit repair costs 5–10%.
projects.oneLiner: Killing the paper checklist at the one moment a customer touches your operation.
projects.problem: The handover is the single moment a customer physically touches your operational reality — and it was run on paper checklists. Paper means no real-time status, no structured damage record, and a workshop that only discovers what it is dealing with when the car is already on the ramp.
approach: Replaced the checklist with a three-step digital protocol, signed on a phone.
Streamed handover status into Salesforce in real time, so operations could see the fleet as it moved.
Built in-app damage reporting with dynamic questionnaires, photos and location sharing — the workshop knew what was coming before the car arrived.
Shipped it MLP-style: a lovable minimum first, then let the numbers grow into the vision.
projects.outcome: 3,700+ digital handovers with 54% at the customer's home, a beta rollout with 100% successful handovers, and per-unit repair costs down 5–10%.
story: The handover is the single moment a customer touches your operational reality. Paper checklists were the norm. We killed them.

A three-step digital protocol, signed on a phone, streamed to Salesforce in real time. In-app damage reporting with dynamic questionnaires, photos, and location sharing so the workshop already knew what it was dealing with when the car arrived. 3,700+ handovers, 54% at the customer's home, and per-unit repair costs down 5–10%. MLP philosophy in practice — ship a lovable minimum, learn, and let the numbers grow into the vision.

projects.title: Operations & Logistics Automation
projects.description: The systems behind lean operations: a work-order management system mapping every job and invoice line item across logistics, maintenance, repair and inspection; OCR-based fine handling from scanned police notice to customer invoice; automated monthly invoicing; on-demand vehicle-health reports; S&OP and mid-mile planning; and the Glide Intake app for VIN-scan check-in. Net effect: over 80% less manual effort on vehicle availability alone.
projects.oneLiner: Fleets don't fail at the exciting parts — so we automated the boring ones.
projects.problem: Fleets fail at the boring parts: a mis-typed VIN, a police notice that never becomes an invoice, a maintenance job nobody billed for. Each one is small; together they cap how large a fleet a lean operations team can run.
approach: Built a work-order management system mapping every job and invoice line item across logistics, maintenance, repair and inspection.
Automated monthly invoicing so billing stopped depending on someone remembering.
Added on-demand vehicle-health reports, so availability was a question the system could answer.
Connected the specialised pieces — OCR fine handling, S&OP planning, mid-mile logistics and Glide intake — into one operating picture.
projects.outcome: Over 80% less manual effort on vehicle availability alone. Not glamorous — very profitable.
story: Fleets don't fail at the exciting parts. They fail at the boring ones — a mis-typed VIN, a police notice that never becomes an invoice, a maintenance job nobody billed for.

So we automated the boring parts. A work-order management system that mapped every job and invoice line across logistics, maintenance, repair, and inspection. OCR that turned a scanned traffic fine into a customer invoice. Automated monthly billing. On-demand vehicle-health reports. S&OP for the fleet, mid-mile planning for the trucks. A Glide app for VIN-scan check-in at intake.
Result: 80%+ less manual effort just on vehicle availability. Not glamorous. Very profitable.

projects.title: Glide Intake — VIN-Scan Vehicle Check-In
projects.description: A mobile app for taking cars in as they arrive at a Cazoo location — scan the VIN to check a vehicle in and confirm its details on the spot, replacing clipboard-and-spreadsheet intake.
projects.oneLiner: Scan a VIN, check the car in — intake in seconds instead of paperwork.
projects.problem: Every car arriving at a hub or refurbishment centre has to be checked in and its details confirmed. Done on paper or in a spreadsheet, that is slow, easy to mistype, and invisible to everyone downstream until someone re-keys it — and a mis-typed VIN follows a vehicle through every system it touches afterwards.
approach: Built a mobile app for intake at the point the car physically arrives, rather than a desk process afterwards.
Made VIN scanning the entry point, so the identifier is captured by the camera instead of typed.
Confirmed vehicle details on the spot, so discrepancies surface while the car is still in front of you.
projects.outcome: Vehicle intake became a scan rather than a form — feeding clean vehicle identity into the logistics and operations systems downstream.

projects.title: Mid-Mile Planning System
projects.description: Planning the middle leg of vehicle logistics for Cazoo — moving whole truckloads of cars between refurbishment centres, distribution hubs and delivery, across European markets.
projects.oneLiner: Hub to hub, truckload by truckload — planning the leg nobody sees.
projects.problem: First mile and last mile get the attention; the middle leg is where the cost sits. Cars have to move between refurbishment centres and distribution hubs in whole truckloads, across markets, and a plan that looks fine on a spreadsheet fails the moment a hub is full or a truck is half empty.
approach: Built planning for the mid-mile leg specifically, rather than treating it as a gap between first and last mile.
Planned at truckload level across refurbishment centres and distribution hubs.
Fitted it to the wider first-mile / mid-mile / last-mile chain being stood up across Germany, France and Spain.
projects.outcome: The middle leg of Cazoo's European vehicle logistics became something that could be planned rather than improvised.

projects.title: OCR Digital Fine Handling
projects.description: Turning a scanned police notice into a customer invoice without a human retyping it — OCR-based traffic-fine handling for a subscription fleet.
projects.oneLiner: Scanned police notice in, customer invoice out — with nobody retyping it.
projects.problem: A subscription fleet collects traffic fines continuously, and each one arrives as a piece of paper naming the operator rather than the driver. Someone has to read it, identify the vehicle and the customer, and raise an invoice. It is pure manual cost, it scales linearly with the fleet, and every notice that falls through the cracks is money the business simply loses.
approach: Used OCR to read the scanned notice instead of having an operator transcribe it.
Matched the notice to the vehicle and the customer responsible at that date automatically.
Carried it straight through to a customer invoice, closing the loop end to end.
projects.outcome: One of the boring, unglamorous processes that quietly caps how large a fleet a lean operations team can run — removed.

projects.title: S&OP Process Automation
projects.description: Sales & operations planning for a growing subscription fleet — automating the process that matches vehicle supply to customer demand.
projects.oneLiner: Matching vehicle supply to customer demand, without the monthly spreadsheet ritual.
projects.problem: A car-subscription business lives or dies on whether the right vehicles are available when customers want them. Get it wrong in one direction and capital sits idle on a lot; get it wrong in the other and you turn customers away. Doing that planning by hand each cycle does not survive growth.
approach: Automated the sales & operations planning cycle instead of rebuilding it in a spreadsheet each period.
Connected vehicle supply and availability to actual customer demand signals.
Fed it into the wider supply-chain and logistics automation across the fleet.
projects.outcome: Supply planning became a system rather than a monthly ritual — part of the lean operations engine behind the subscription fleet.
projects.coverCaption: planning the fleet, not the spreadsheet

projects.title: ZEISS AI Box — Robotic Inspection Cell
projects.description: Robot-mounted optical measurement cell inspecting car-body parts next to the production line for Carl Zeiss IMT. Product owner, application engineer and software release manager from hardware & software requirements to release — piloted at Porsche Weissach and Daimler Sindelfingen, with cells in Germany, Shanghai and Detroit.
projects.oneLiner: A robot, a Zeiss camera and a live production line — optical inspection where the cars are actually built.
projects.role: Product Owner, Application Engineer & Software Release Manager
projects.problem: Car-body parts were measured away from the line, which means delay between making a part and knowing whether it was good. Moving optical measurement next to production means a robot, a camera and a dozen software components have to agree — and measurement is unforgiving: if one link in the chain lies, the whole result is a lie.
approach: Took requirements in the room at Porsche Weissach and Daimler Sindelfingen rather than from a spec document.
Got FANUC-certified to programme the robot personally, then mounted a ZEISS camera on it.
Owned hardware and software requirements through to release as product owner, application engineer and release manager.
Ran 'LAN parties' when things broke — engineers from every geography in one room, one problem, one week.
projects.outcome: Cells piloted at Porsche and Daimler, and shipped in Germany, Shanghai and Detroit.
story: This project put me on airplanes. Porsche in Weissach. Daimler in Sindelfingen. Understand the requirement in the room, not in a spec doc. Get FANUC-certified so I could programme the robot myself. Mount a Zeiss camera on it. Drop the whole cell into a live production line.

The technical challenge was systems integration at its purest — a plethora of software components had to talk to each other, and every one of them had to work. Measurement is unforgiving; if one link in the chain lies, the whole result is a lie.

When things broke, I ran what I called LAN parties — engineers from every geography in one room, one problem, one week. Leading people to solve a problem, not managing tickets. We failed as a team. We succeeded as a team. That's the frame I still lead by.
Cells shipped in Germany, Shanghai, and Detroit.

projects.title: ZEISS Reverse Engineering — CAD Suite
projects.description: ZEISS Reverse Engineering — CAD reverse engineering and tool correction for mould making, built on point-cloud processing and BRep modelling (ACIS kernel). Technical lead from the first line of code at TCS, then owner through requirements, architecture, release, sales and support at MERZ for Carl Zeiss IMT. Followed by Merz CAD Workmate, an in-house CAD app later ported to Android and Microsoft HoloLens for holographic on-part reverse engineering.
projects.oneLiner: From a professor's algorithm to holograms — six years, two companies, one CAD product.
projects.role: Technical lead → product owner (requirements to sales & support)
projects.problem: A mathematics professor had an algorithm that extracted surfaces from point clouds, so a physical part could be compared against its original CAD design. Turning that into a product mould-makers could rely on — reverse engineering and tool correction, robust enough to sell and support — was an entirely different problem from proving the maths.
approach: Wrote the first line of the new system, learning C#, WPF, MVVM, .NET and agile simultaneously.
Built point-cloud processing and BRep modelling on the ACIS kernel for reverse engineering and tool correction in mould making.
Hired and led the team in Bangalore — 12 engineers, then 25.
Rebuilt the product from scratch at MERZ with clean architecture and a smaller, stronger team, then owned it through requirements, architecture, release, sales and support.
Extended it into Merz CAD Workmate, ported to Android and Microsoft HoloLens for holographic, on-part reverse engineering.
projects.outcome: A product that carried Carl Zeiss IMT's reverse engineering for years — and the experience that taught me to trust work over words.
story: First trip to Germany. Twenty-something years old. Handed the code of a mathematics professor — Dr. Deets — whose algorithm extracted surfaces from point clouds so you could compare a physical part against its original CAD design.

I wrote the first line of the new system. Learned C#, WPF, MVVM, the .NET framework, agile — everything new, all at once, and I loved every minute of it. Back in Bangalore I hired the rest of the team: 12, then 25 engineers. Some of them were sharp enough to find flaws in the code I'd already written. That ego bruise turned out to be the fastest way to learn.

By 2013 my company was pushing to grow the team when I knew the product needed fewer, better people. I left. The client called the next day. I joined Merz Group and rebuilt the whole thing from scratch — clean architecture, right team, my call.

Working with Germans permanently changed how I evaluate people. In India, if you asked someone 'do you know X?' and they knew 10%, they'd say yes. In Germany, if they knew 99% but not 100%, they'd say no. I stopped trusting words. I trust work.

Later this became Merz CAD Workmate — an in-house CAD app we ported to Android and Microsoft HoloLens for holographic, on-part reverse engineering. From a professor's algorithm to holograms, in six years.
projects.coverCaption: TCS → MERZ, ZEISS Reverse Engineering from scratch

projects.title: ZEISS Caligo & Adaptive Clamping
projects.description: Two projects that turned me from a software person into a product person: Caligo DMS, a laser-projection measurement system where I first learned to solutionize with customers, and ROLEX — a universal clamping-pin field that adapts itself to any freeform part, computing per-pin Z-shifts from the CAD contour so the fixture physically reshapes to hold what it is about to machine.
projects.oneLiner: The project that turned a software person into a product person — plus a fixture that reshapes itself.
projects.problem: Caligo DMS was a laser-projection measurement system that almost worked — and customers had stopped handing over requirements. They were showing daily friction instead. Separately, holding freeform parts for machining meant a bespoke fixture per part, which is slow and expensive.
approach: Stopped executing specifications and started solutionising with customers in front of the real problem.
Turned that into work packages clean enough that engineers just built, with no back-and-forth.
Designed ROLEX, a universal clamping-pin field that adapts to any freeform part — computing per-pin Z-shifts from the CAD contour so the fixture physically reshapes around what it is about to hold.
Built it as modular libraries reusable across products, from feasibility prototype to delivery plan.
projects.outcome: A fixture that reforms itself for any part — and the point where I stopped calling myself a software person and became a product person who could still write code.
story: Caligo doesn't look like the biggest project on this page, but it's the one that changed my identity.

Customers weren't handing me requirements anymore. They were showing me their pain — the daily friction of working with a laser-projection measurement system that almost worked. For the first time I stopped executing and started solutionizing with them, then coming back to the team with a work package clean enough that engineers just built, no back-and-forth.
That's when I stopped calling myself a software person. I was a product person who could still write code.

In parallel, ROLEX: a universal clamping-pin field that shape-shifts to any freeform part. Compute the CAD contour, project per-pin Z-shifts, and the fixture literally reforms itself to hold whatever's about to be machined. Modular libraries, reusable across products, from feasibility prototype to delivery plan.
projects.coverCaption: CAD contour → per-pin Z-shift, zero rework

projects.title: MERZ CAD Workmate — Cross-Platform & AR/VR CAD
projects.description: Architect and product manager for a cross-platform CAD application with AR/VR support — later ported to Android and Microsoft HoloLens for holographic, on-part reverse engineering.
projects.oneLiner: CAD off the workstation and onto the part — cross-platform, and in holograms.
projects.problem: CAD lives on a workstation, but the part it describes lives on the shop floor. Every time an engineer has to walk between the two, the comparison happens from memory. Getting CAD onto the floor means a cross-platform application — and eventually a headset that puts the model on the part itself.
approach: Architected an in-house CAD application that ran across platforms rather than one workstation.
Designed it for AR/VR devices from the outset instead of retrofitting a viewer.
Ported it to Android and Microsoft HoloLens for holographic, on-part reverse engineering.
projects.outcome: The point where a professor's point-cloud algorithm ended up as a hologram overlaid on the physical part.

projects.title: ML Defect Detection for CT Scans
projects.description: I was training neural networks for industrial inspection in 2017 — years before AI became fashionable. Machine-learning defect detection (Caffe) on computed-tomography scans of precision components for semiconductor manufacturing: volumetric scan import, defect classification by probability, type, size and rest-wall thickness, and a trainable master/user workflow where engineers teach the model new defect classes. Project lead from requirement definition through delivery.
projects.oneLiner: Training neural networks for industrial inspection in 2017 — years before AI was fashionable.
projects.problem: Precision pipes for semiconductor manufacturing had to be checked for micro-defects. A trained human spent a week per batch squinting at computed-tomography scans — slow, expensive, and inconsistent in exactly the way a person gets tired.
approach: Trained a Caffe model on labelled defects, classifying by probability, type, size and rest-wall thickness.
Built volumetric scan import so CT data went straight into the pipeline.
Designed a trainable master/user workflow so engineers could teach the model new defect classes as they appeared in production.
Led the project from requirement definition through delivery, with Fraunhofer researchers advocating for neural nets harder than I did.
projects.outcome: It worked — despite near-universal scepticism at the time. My first AI project, eight years before the rest of the industry arrived.
story: My first AI project. 2017. Pre-Transformer, pre-hype. In collaboration with Fraunhofer, whose researchers advocated for neural nets harder than I did.

The problem: precision pipes for semiconductor manufacturing had to be inspected for micro-defects. A trained human spent a week per batch, squinting at CT scans. We trained a Caffe model on labelled defects — probability, type, size, rest-wall thickness — with a master/user workflow so an engineer could teach the model new defect classes as they appeared in production.

Every time I told someone what I was working on, they thought it wouldn't work. It worked. That's when the 2008 daydream came back to me — a world where you type in English and machines write code. Fifteen years early. But the direction was right.

projects.title: Product & Engineering Leadership
projects.description: Building and leading cross-functional teams across engineering, product, and design — from three departments at MERZ to app teams at AutoScout24 — hiring, delivery cadence, and a bias toward shipping useful software over slideware.
projects.oneLiner: Seven teams, seven geographies, one product — and the operating rule underneath all of it.
projects.role: Head of Software → Head of Product / Head of Digital Solutions
projects.problem: Leading software people is mostly not a software problem. Across three departments at MERZ, app teams at AutoScout24 and product teams at Cluno, Cazoo and CUBONIC, the recurring question is the same: how do you keep people motivated and aligned across time zones, and how do you hire so that shipping is the default?
approach: Led seven teams across seven geographies on one product after being promoted to Head of Software at MERZ at 25.
Hired against three signals every time: is this person telling the truth about their CV, can they think under pressure, and can they communicate.
Built on three pillars — Transparency → Trust → Positivity.
Applied one operating rule: judge people by what they ship, not what they promise, then give them the room to ship.
projects.outcome: Teams that shipped useful software instead of slideware, across industrial metrology, mobility marketplaces and AI.
story: Promoted to Head of Software at Merz at 25 — not because I was close to the CEO, but because I'd shown him what the group could do beyond one or two customers. Seven teams, seven geographies, one product. That's where I learned that keeping people motivated across time zones is the actual job.

Since then: PMs and engineers at Cluno, Cazoo, AutoScout24, and CUBONIC. Same hiring signal every time — is this person telling the truth about their CV, can they think under pressure, and can they communicate? Genius that can't communicate loses to competence that can.

The way I lead sits on three pillars: Transparency → Trust → Positivity. And underneath all of it, one operating rule: judge people by what they ship, not what they promise. Then give them the room to ship.
